{{Short description|Equation in Brownian motion}}
In [[physics]] (specifically, the [[kinetic theory of gases]]), the '''Einstein relation''' is a previously unexpected{{what|date=September 2023|reason=Exactly what was unexpected?}} connection revealed independently by [[William Sutherland (physicist)|William Sutherland]] in 1904,<!-- 
With the use of the word "revealed", we should use 1904 for Sutherland:
"Sutherland reported his solution to this problem in 1904 in a paper at the year."
The original revelation (and indeed, arguably, publication) by Sutherland was thus in 1904, irrespective of the fact that this was not in the form of a journal article.  
--><ref>[http://www.ph.unimelb.edu.au/~dnj/wyop/wyop2005-sutherland-essay.html World Year of Physics – William Sutherland at the University of Melbourne]. Essay by Prof. R Home (with contributions from Prof B. McKellar and A./Prof D. Jamieson) dated 2005.  Accessed 2017-04-28.</ref><ref>{{cite journal | doi = 10.1080/14786440509463331 | volume=9 | issue=54 | title=LXXV. A dynamical theory of diffusion for non-electrolytes and the molecular mass of albumin | year=1905 | journal=Philosophical Magazine |series=Series 6 | pages=781–785 | author=Sutherland William| url=https://zenodo.org/record/1430774 }}</ref><ref>P. Hänggi, [http://www.physik.uni-augsburg.de/theo1/hanggi/History/Robert_Brown_Vortrag.pdf "Stokes–Einstein–Sutherland equation"].</ref> [[Albert Einstein]] in 1905,<ref>{{cite journal
|author=Einstein, A {{IPAc-en|}}
|title=Über die von der molekularkinetischen Theorie der Wärme geforderte Bewegung von in ruhenden Flüssigkeiten suspendierten Teilchen
|journal=Annalen der Physik
|volume=322
|issue=8
|pages=549–560
|year=1905
|language=de
|doi=10.1002/andp.19053220806 |bibcode = 1905AnP...322..549E |url=http://sedici.unlp.edu.ar/handle/10915/2785
|doi-access=free
}}</ref> and by [[Marian Smoluchowski]] in 1906<ref>{{cite journal
|author=von Smoluchowski, M.
|title=Zur kinetischen Theorie der Brownschen Molekularbewegung und der Suspensionen
|journal=Annalen der Physik
|volume=326
|issue=14
|pages=756–780
|year=1906
|language=de
|doi=10.1002/andp.19063261405 |bibcode = 1906AnP...326..756V |url=https://zenodo.org/record/1424073
}}</ref> in their works on [[Brownian motion]]. The more general form of the equation in the classical case is<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hdeODhjp1bUC&pg=PA327 |title=Molecular Driving Forces: Statistical Thermodynamics in Chemistry and Biology |last1=Dill |first1=Ken A. |last2=Bromberg |first2=Sarina |date=2003 |publisher=Garland Science |isbn=9780815320517 |pages=327 |language=en}}</ref>

<math display="block"> D = \mu \, k_\text{B} T, </math>
where
* {{mvar|D}} is the [[Mass diffusivity|diffusion coefficient]];
* {{mvar|μ}} is the "mobility", or the ratio of the particle's [[Terminal velocity|terminal]] [[drift velocity]] to an applied [[force]], {{math|1=''μ'' = ''v''<sub>d</sub>/''F''}};
* {{math|''k''<sub>B</sub>}} is the [[Boltzmann constant]];
* {{mvar|T}} is the [[absolute temperature]].

This equation is an early example of a [[fluctuation dissipation theorem|fluctuation-dissipation relation]].<ref>Umberto Marini Bettolo Marconi, Andrea Puglisi, Lamberto Rondoni, Angelo Vulpiani, [https://arxiv.org/abs/0803.0719 "Fluctuation-Dissipation: Response Theory in Statistical Physics"].</ref>
Note that the equation above describes the classical case and should be modified when quantum effects are relevant. 

Two frequently used important special forms of the relation are:

* '''Einstein–Smoluchowski equation''', for diffusion of [[electric charge|charged]] particles:<ref>Van Zeghbroeck, "Principles of Semiconductor Devices", [http://ecee.colorado.edu/~bart/book/book/chapter2/ch2_7.htm Chapter 2.7] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210506163214/http://ecee.colorado.edu/~bart/book/book/chapter2/ch2_7.htm |date=2021-05-06 }}.</ref> <math display="block">D = \frac{\mu_q \, k_\text{B} T}{q}</math>
* '''Stokes–Einstein–Sutherland equation''', for diffusion of spherical particles through a liquid with low [[Reynolds number]]: <math display="block">D = \frac{k_\text{B} T}{6\pi\,\eta\,r} </math>

Here
* {{mvar|q}} is the [[electrical charge]] of a particle;
* {{math|''μ<sub>q</sub>''}} is the [[electrical mobility]] of the charged particle;
* {{mvar|η}} is the dynamic [[viscosity]];
* {{mvar|r}} is the [[Stokes radius]] of the spherical particle.

==Special cases==

===Electrical mobility equation (classical case)===

For a particle with [[electrical charge]] {{mvar|q}}, its [[electrical mobility]] {{math|''μ<sub>q</sub>''}} is related to its generalized mobility {{mvar|μ}} by the equation {{math|1=''μ'' = ''μ<sub>q</sub>''/''q''}}. The parameter {{math|''μ<sub>q</sub>''}} is the ratio of the particle's terminal [[drift velocity]] to an applied [[electric field]]. Hence, the equation in the case of a charged particle is given as
<math display="block">D = \frac{\mu_q \, k_\text{B} T}{q},</math>

where
* <math>D</math> is the diffusion coefficient (<math>\mathrm{m^2 s^{-1}}</math>).
* <math>\mu_q</math> is the [[electrical mobility]] (<math>\mathrm{m^2 V^{-1} s^{-1}}</math>).
* <math>q</math> is the [[electric charge]] of particle (C, coulombs)
* <math>T</math> is the electron temperature or ion temperature in plasma (K).<ref>{{Cite book |title=Gas Discharge Physics |last=Raizer |first=Yuri |publisher=Springer |year=2001 |isbn=978-3540194620 |pages=20–28}}</ref>

If the temperature is given in [[Volt|volts]], which is more common for plasma:
<math display="block">D = \frac{\mu_q \, T}{Z},</math>
where
* <math>Z</math> is the [[charge number]] of particle (unitless)
* <math>T</math> is electron temperature or ion temperature in plasma (V).

===Electrical mobility equation (quantum case)===
For the case of [[Fermi gas]] or a [[Fermi liquid theory|Fermi liquid]], relevant for the electron mobility in normal metals like in the [[free electron model]], Einstein relation should be modified:
<math display="block">D = \frac{\mu_q \, E_{\mathrm F}}{q},</math>
where <math>E_{\mathrm F}</math> is [[Fermi energy]].

=== Stokes–Einstein–Sutherland equation ===

In the limit of low [[Reynolds number]], the mobility ''μ'' is the inverse of the drag coefficient <math>\zeta</math>. A damping constant <math>\gamma = \zeta / m</math> is frequently used for the inverse momentum relaxation time (time needed for the inertia momentum to become negligible compared to the random momenta) of the diffusive object. For spherical particles of radius ''r'', [[Stokes' law]] gives
<math display="block">\zeta = 6 \pi \, \eta \, r,</math>
where <math>\eta</math> is the [[viscosity]] of the medium. Thus the Einstein–Smoluchowski relation results into the Stokes–Einstein–Sutherland relation
<math display="block">D = \frac{k_\text{B} T}{6\pi\,\eta\,r}.</math>
This has been applied for many years to estimating the self-diffusion coefficient in liquids, and a version consistent with isomorph theory has been confirmed by computer simulations of the [[Lennard-Jones potential|Lennard-Jones]] system.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Costigliola|first1=Lorenzo|last2=Heyes|first2=David M.|last3=Schrøder|first3=Thomas B.|last4=Dyre|first4=Jeppe C.| date=2019-01-14|title=Revisiting the Stokes-Einstein relation without a hydrodynamic diameter|journal=The Journal of Chemical Physics |language=en|volume=150|issue=2|pages=021101|doi=10.1063/1.5080662|pmid=30646717|bibcode=2019JChPh.150b1101C |issn=0021-9606|doi-access=free|url=http://glass.ruc.dk/pdf/articles/2019_JChemPhys_150_021101.pdf}}</ref> 

In the case of [[rotational diffusion]], the friction is <math>\zeta_\text{r} = 8 \pi \eta r^3</math>, and the rotational diffusion constant <math>D_\text{r}</math> is
<math display="block">D_\text{r} = \frac{k_\text{B} T}{8\pi\,\eta\,r^3}.</math>
This is sometimes referred to as the Stokes–Einstein–Debye relation.

===Semiconductor===
In a [[semiconductor]] with an arbitrary [[density of states]], i.e. a relation of the form <math>p = p(\varphi)</math> between the density of holes or electrons <math>p</math> and the corresponding [[quasi Fermi level]] (or [[electrochemical potential]]) <math>\varphi</math>, the Einstein relation is<ref>{{cite book
|author1=Ashcroft, N. W. |author2=Mermin, N. D.
|title=Solid State Physics
|pages=826
|year=1988
|publisher=Holt, Rineheart and Winston
|place=New York (USA)}}</ref><ref>{{cite book
|author=Bonnaud, Olivier
|title=Composants à semiconducteurs
|pages=78
|year=2006
|publisher=Ellipses
|place=Paris (France)
|language=fr}}</ref>
<math display="block">D = \frac{\mu_q p}{q \frac{dp}{d\varphi}},</math>
where <math>\mu_q</math> is the [[electrical mobility]] (see {{slink||Proof of the general case}} for a proof of this relation). An example assuming a [[Density of states#Parabolic dispersion|parabolic dispersion]] relation for the density of states and the [[Maxwell–Boltzmann statistics]], which is often used to describe [[inorganic compound|inorganic]] [[semiconductor]] materials, one can compute (see [[Density of states#Density of states and distribution functions|density of states]]):
<math display="block">p(\varphi) = N_0 e^{\frac{q \varphi}{k_\text{B} T}},</math>
where <math>N_0</math> is the total density of available energy states, which gives the simplified relation:
<math display="block">D = \mu_q \frac{k_\text{B} T}{q}.</math>

=== Nernst–Einstein equation ===
By replacing the diffusivities in the expressions of electric ionic mobilities of the cations and anions from the expressions of the [[equivalent conductivity]] of an electrolyte the Nernst–Einstein equation is derived:
<math display="block">\Lambda_e = \frac{z_i^2 F^2}{RT}(D_+ +  D_-).</math>were ''R'' is the [[gas constant]].

==Proof of the general case==
The proof of the Einstein relation can be found in many references, for example see the work of [[Ryogo Kubo]].<ref>{{cite journal
|author=Kubo, R.
|title=The fluctuation-dissipation theorem
|journal=[[Rep. Prog. Phys.]]
|volume=29
|issue=1
|pages=255–284
|year=1966
|bibcode = 1966RPPh...29..255K |doi = 10.1088/0034-4885/29/1/306 |s2cid=250892844
|arxiv=0710.4394
}}</ref> The following derives it from the steady state of the [[convection-diffusion equation#Velocity in response to a force|convection-diffusion equation]] with a velocity proportional to a conservative force.

Suppose some fixed, external [[potential energy]] <math>U</math> generates a [[conservative force]] <math>F(\mathbf{x})=-\nabla U(\mathbf{x})</math> (for example, an electric force) on a particle located at a given position <math>\mathbf{x}</math>. We assume that the particle would respond by moving with velocity <math>v(\mathbf{x})=\mu(\mathbf{x}) F(\mathbf{x})</math> (see [[Drag (physics)]]). Now assume that there are a large number of such particles, with local concentration <math>\rho(\mathbf{x})</math> as a function of the position. After some time, equilibrium will be established: particles will pile up around the areas with lowest potential energy <math>U</math>, but still will be spread out to some extent because of [[diffusion]]. At equilibrium, there is no net flow of particles: the tendency of particles to get pulled towards lower <math>U</math>, called the ''drift current'', perfectly balances the tendency of particles to spread out due to diffusion, called the ''diffusion current''.

The net flux of particles due to the drift current is
<math display="block">\mathbf{J}_\mathrm{drift}(\mathbf{x}) = \mu(\mathbf{x}) F(\mathbf{x}) \rho(\mathbf{x}) = -\rho(\mathbf{x}) \mu(\mathbf{x}) \nabla U(\mathbf{x}),</math>
i.e., the number of particles flowing past a given position equals the particle concentration times the average velocity.

The flow of particles due to the diffusion current is, by [[Fick's law]],
<math display="block">\mathbf{J}_\mathrm{diffusion}(\mathbf{x})=-D(\mathbf{x}) \nabla \rho(\mathbf{x}),</math>
where the minus sign means that particles flow from higher to lower concentration.

Now consider the equilibrium condition. First, there is no net flow, i.e. <math>\mathbf{J}_\mathrm{drift} + \mathbf{J}_\mathrm{diffusion} = 0</math>. Second, for non-interacting point particles, the equilibrium density <math>\rho</math> is solely a function of the local potential energy <math>U</math>, i.e. if two locations have the same <math>U</math> then they will also have the same <math>\rho</math> (e.g. see [[Maxwell-Boltzmann statistics]] as discussed below.) That means, applying the [[chain rule]],
<math display="block">\nabla\rho = \frac{\mathrm{d}\rho}{\mathrm{d} U} \nabla U.</math>

Therefore, at equilibrium:
<math display="block">0 = \mathbf{J}_\mathrm{drift} + \mathbf{J}_\mathrm{diffusion} = -\mu \rho \nabla U - D \nabla \rho = \left(-\mu \rho - D \frac{\mathrm{d}\rho}{\mathrm{d} U}\right)\nabla U.</math>

As this expression holds at every position <math>\mathbf{x}</math>, it implies the general form of the Einstein relation:
<math display="block">D = -\mu \frac{\rho}{\frac{\mathrm{d}\rho}{\mathrm{d} U}}.</math>

The relation between <math>\rho</math> and <math>U</math> for [[Classical physics|classical particles]] can be modeled through [[Maxwell-Boltzmann statistics]]
<math display="block">\rho(\mathbf{x}) = A e^{-\frac{U(\mathbf{x})}{k_\text{B} T}},</math>
where <math>A</math> is a constant related to the total number of particles. Therefore
<math display="block">\frac{\mathrm{d}\rho}{\mathrm{d} U} = -\frac{1}{k_\text{B} T}\rho.</math>

Under this assumption, plugging this equation into the general Einstein relation gives:
<math display="block">D = -\mu \frac{\rho}{\frac{\mathrm{d}\rho}{\mathrm{d} U}} = \mu k_\text{B} T,</math>
which corresponds to the classical Einstein relation.
